summary: Defines the not-so-stubby area (NSSA), an OSPF area type that behaves like a stub area but can still import a limited set of external routes. This helps sites that attach outside networks to an otherwise simple area. It was a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 3101.

plainLanguage.summary: A small neighborhood normally blocks outside traffic. This lets one gate stay open so a few outside roads can connect. It has since been replaced by a newer design.

subtitle: OSPF areas that import external routes within limits.

tldr.problem: OSPF stub areas prevent external routing information from flooding into the area, reducing overhead. But sometimes a site needs to import a few external routes (from RIP or other protocols) while staying lightweight.
tldr.mechanism: The Not-So-Stubby Area (NSSA) is a new area type that acts like a stub area but allows internal routers to originate type-7 LSAs for external routes. Area border routers translate selected type-7 LSAs into type-5 LSAs and flood them to the rest of the OSPF system.
tldr.outcome: Stub-like areas can now import external routes, reducing the need for non-OSPF protocols or non-stub area configuration. The RFC was proposed but later refined by RFC 3101.

facts.label: Area scope
facts.value: Type-7 LSAs do not leave the NSSA

today: RFC 1587 was a Proposed Standard that defined the NSSA option for OSPF. The approach worked but had some limitations. It was later superseded by RFC 3101, which provides a more complete and refined specification.

sections.title: Introduction to OSPF Areas
sections.content:
OSPF is a routing protocol that divides networks into areas to reduce the size of routing databases. An area is a set of networks under local administration, and routers within an area know each other's full topology. The backbone area (area 0) connects all other areas.

OSPF defines stub areas as areas that do not receive or originate external routes (type-5 LSAs). Stub areas are simpler and have smaller routing tables, which is useful for leaf networks far from the backbone. However, stub areas cannot import external routing information from other protocols like RIP, a limitation for sites that need to advertise some external networks.

This RFC introduces the Not-So-Stubby Area (NSSA), a new area type that retains the simplicity of stub areas but allows limited external routing.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF divides networks into areas to make routing simpler. Stub areas hide external routes, making them very light. NSSAs are stub areas that can peek outside.

sections.title: The Problem: Stub Areas and External Routes
sections.content:
Wide-area networks like NSFNET often connect to leaf sites that run older routing protocols like RIP internally. A leaf site might have multiple IP networks, but from the transit network's perspective, it is a single stub entity with one exit point.

In the traditional OSPF model, a stub area is ideal for such a topology: it reduces routing overhead and the leaf site does not need to know about all external routes in the backbone. But there is a catch: a stub area cannot import any external routes, even from the leaf site itself. If the leaf site runs RIP and needs to advertise its internal networks back into OSPF, the site must either:

  • Use a non-stub area, which requires the leaf router to learn all backbone external routes (expensive).
  • Run OSPF only out to a boundary router and use RIP between the boundary router and the leaf (no longer purely OSPF).

This is the fundamental limitation that NSSAs address.
sections.plainLanguage: A site with its own networks needs to tell the backbone about them, but stub areas do not allow this. Routers have to choose between hiding too much or learning too much.

sections.title: The NSSA Solution
sections.content:
An NSSA behaves like a stub area but adds the ability to originate and propagate type-7 LSAs (external link-state advertisements) within the area. Type-7 LSAs are identical to type-5 LSAs in format but are area-scoped: they flood only within the NSSA, not to the backbone or other areas.

To support NSSAs, the RFC introduces:

  • The N-bit in Hello packets, which ensures all routers in an NSSA agree the area is an NSSA. Like the E-bit for stub areas, if the N-bit disagrees between neighbors, they do not form an adjacency.
  • Type-7 LSAs, which are originated by internal AS boundary routers (routers connected to external networks like RIP). Type-7 LSAs include a P-bit (propagate bit) that flags whether an area border router should translate the LSA to type-5.

An NSSA area border router examines type-7 LSAs and translates selected ones into type-5 LSAs. This allows the backbone and other areas to learn external routes from the NSSA without the NSSA itself receiving full type-5 LSA flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: NSSAs use a new kind of route announcement (type-7) that stays inside the area. The exit router picks which ones to advertise to the rest of OSPF, converting them to the standard format (type-5).

sections.title: Type-7 LSAs and Border Router Translation
sections.content:
An NSSA internal AS boundary router (a router with a connection to an external routing domain like RIP) originates type-7 LSAs for external networks. If the router wants the network to be translated and advertised to the backbone, it sets the P-bit in the LSA header and provides a valid forwarding address.

The NSSA area border router (the router that connects the NSSA to the backbone) is responsible for translating type-7 LSAs to type-5 LSAs. It can be configured with type-7 address ranges, which allow multiple type-7 routes to be summarized into a single type-5 LSA. For example, a router might summarize all type-7 routes in the 10.0.0.0/8 range into a single type-5 advertisement.

The translation algorithm ensures loop avoidance: only the area border router with the highest router ID performs translation, and the P-bit prevents the same route from being translated twice.

Unlike stub areas, NSSAs must receive all type-3 LSAs (summary routes for OSPF internal networks). This ensures that internal OSPF routes are preferred over external type-7 routes. An NSSA area border router can also originate a default type-7 route (0.0.0.0) to provide a default path to external destinations.
sections.plainLanguage: Internal routers announce external networks as type-7 routes. The boundary router picks which ones to announce to the backbone, optionally grouping them into larger summaries to save space.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 1587 was a Proposed Standard that introduced the NSSA option to OSPF. The concept was useful but the specification had some rough edges. It was later refined and superseded by RFC 3101, which clarified the mechanisms and fixed issues in the translation algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: This was the first version of NSSAs. A later RFC cleaned up the design based on implementation experience.

layers.label: Backbone (Area 0)
layers.detail: Sees type-5 LSAs translated from NSSA

layers.label: External Domain
layers.detail: RIP or other protocols inside the NSSA
